did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah was sent specifically to the royal palace so that the divine message would be heard by the king of Judah, his servants, and the people living in Jerusalem.

Did you know? The king’s central responsibility was to practice justice and righteousness and protect the vulnerable—the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow—and to rescue the oppressed from their oppressors.
Did you know? According to the prophecy, the continuation of David’s descendants on the throne depended on moral conduct and obedience to the word of the Lord, not merely on their dynastic right.

Did you know? The prophecy describes a time when many nations would ask why Jerusalem was destroyed, and the answer would be that the people had abandoned the Lord’s covenant and turned to worship other gods.

Did you know? Jeremiah distinguishes between mourning for a king who has died and weeping for a king who is going into exile. The one going into exile should be mourned because he will never return to see his native land.
Did you know? Jehoiakim is portrayed as building his house through exploitation: he makes his countrymen work without pay and refuses to give his laborers what they are owed.

Did you know? Josiah, Jehoiakim’s father, is presented as an example of a king who practiced justice and righteousness and defended the cause of the poor and needy. For this, it is said that he knew the Lord.
Did you know? It is said of Jehoiakim that he would not receive the usual mourning given to kings. Instead, his burial is described as the burial of a donkey—a powerful image of disgrace after death.

Did you know? Coniah is compared to a signet ring on the Lord’s right hand, yet despite the ring’s symbolic value, the Lord declares that he will tear him from his position and hand him over to his enemies.

Did you know? The designation “childless” at the end of the chapter is explained by the fact that none of Coniah’s descendants would succeed in sitting on David’s throne and ruling in Judah. The verse focuses on the failure of the royal succession.
